title: Nobody's Name
aliases: The Hill of the Quiet Mind
logline: One rock overhang, wide enough and deep enough that people have said it could shelter a small town, was lived under for something on the order of forty thousand years, and of everyone who lived under it not one can be named: no inscription, no chronicle, no lineage, no tradition. Their names were said here every day, and none of them was kept. What is left is ash, quartz chips, freshwater shell, and a shark's tooth carried a long way in from the sea.
human_question: If tens of thousands of people lived under one rock and there is no name here for any of them, what exactly do I think a name is fastened to when I use my own?

place.what_kind_of_place: A single enormous overhang bitten out of a gneiss cliff in lowland rainforest, two hundred metres or so above the valleys, reached on foot up a long flight of stone steps through rubber and secondary forest. The mouth faces east. The published field measurements give it roughly thirty metres across and twenty metres of clear height above the floor, with the shelter running back about ten metres into the cliff; popular accounts give much larger figures and a capacity of three thousand people, and the two sets of numbers do not agree. Inside it is one continuous dry floor of packed dust and stone, a curved roof of raw water-worn rock overhead, and darkness at the back that daylight never reaches. Part of the floor is occupied by a modern shrine with a large reclining figure and a monk's dwelling built against the rock. Part of it is an archaeological excavation: an open pit with timber shoring, railings around it, and two or three grinding stones set out on low plinths. There is nothing carved into this rock anywhere, and nothing written on it.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things, and only three, and none of them requires the camera to move. First, the single frame from inside looking out: the arch of the overhang filling the entire top of the picture, the opening blazing with forest and sky, the floor running away to the drip line, and one person standing down there small enough that the rock finally reads at its true size. It is one of the largest single held frames any location in this series can give. Second, the light, which is a clock with one hand: the mouth faces east, so for the first couple of hours after sunrise a hard slab of light lies across the floor and rakes the rock, and then it leaves, and the whole interior settles into a flat, even, shadowless grey that does not change again all day. Third, the opposite extreme: the cut face of the excavation, where ash, dark loam and pebbly silt are stacked in legible bands, and the small hard things themselves, a quartz flake with a fresh edge on it, a grinding stone with ochre still in the dish, at a magnification where they stop looking like objects and start looking like material.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, which is the point and the discipline. The film is built out of long static takes and the only movement permitted in a frame is movement that belongs to the place. The slab of morning light crosses the floor and withdraws. Dust hangs in it. In the wet months a curtain of rain falls past the mouth, lit, while the floor two metres inside it stays dry and grey. Swifts or bats may cross the opening; they are not baited or waited for. A visitor walks into the wide frame, stands, and walks out, and their entire function in the film is scale. There is no aerial shot, no crane, no push in, no rack focus used as a reveal, and no drone payoff at all. Wide and macro, and almost nothing in between.
place.when_it_looks_best: The drier window, roughly January to March, when the steps are passable and the forest is not leeching; the southwest monsoon from May to September and the second wet spell around October will hand the film its rain curtain and also its worst access. Time of day matters more than season: the east-facing mouth means the raking light and the shadow-filled rock texture exist only in the first hours after sunrise, and the shelter is in even, usable, unchanging shade from mid-morning onward, which is exactly what the long static interiors and the macro work want.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A very quiet, very large film about a hole in a rock. Steps up through wet forest; the cliff coming into view through the canopy; the overhang from below; then inside, and the one enormous held frame that tells you how big it is; the light crossing the floor and going; the dark at the back; and then the film changes scale completely and spends its second half about ten centimetres from a wall of stacked sediment and a chipped piece of quartz. It resolves without a word: outside to inside, huge to tiny, morning to flat afternoon. Somebody who never hears the narration gets a complete piece with a build and a payoff, and the payoff is the sudden change of scale rather than any event.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the compendium with its subject removed. The voice never contradicts what is on screen and never asks the viewer to imagine anybody. It points at what is actually there: layers, ash, chips, a tooth from a sea fish, carried in from a coast that today lies some thirty kilometres away. The sources define a name as one half of a pair, the thing made known and the means of making it known, and they say the concept of a being is formed with the five aggregates as its basis. At this site what those people handled is on the table and every designation is missing. Names were certainly used here; none was kept, because nothing here could keep one. Not erased, not mourned: not kept. And what a name for a person rests on, by the sources' account, is not on the table either and could not be. The film's claim is that anonymity here is a condition of the evidence, and that the analysis the compendium performs on a person, taking the name off and looking, can be watched here with no name available to take off.

sequence.on_screen: Static, from inside the shelter looking out, held far longer than is comfortable. The arch of the overhang occupies the whole top of the frame in silhouette; the opening is white with daylight and forest; the dry floor runs away to the drip line. One person stands near the mouth, small. Nothing in the frame moves except leaves outside.
sequence.voice: People lived under this rock for tens of thousands of years, and not one of them can be named. There is no inscription here, no chronicle, no donor list, no lineage, nothing cut into the stone at all. The texts have a word for a name, and they define it twice over in one sentence: a convention, other than mind and matter, which is both the thing that is made known and the means of making it known. Under this rock, the second half of that sentence is the half that did not survive.

sequence.on_screen: Cut to the opposite extreme. Macro, static, very slow: the cut face of the excavation, timber shoring at the edge of frame. Pale ash, dark loam, pebbly silt, another band of ash, stacked across the picture. The shot is held until the eye starts reading it downward on its own.
sequence.voice: This is the floor they lived on, cut through. Ash, silt, chips of quartz, burnt bone, ash again. The compendium these films come from opens by sorting everything that exists into five heaps, then into twelve bases, then eighteen elements, then four truths, and it is careful about the word heap: it means a collection, a portion, and not a label. All the materiality there has ever been, divided as past and future and present, is taken by the mind as one collection and called by one word. That is what a wall of layers is.

sequence.on_screen: Macro, static: the rock itself where water has worked it, fluted and stained, the surface of the overhang just above the old floor level. Long hold. The only change is a slow strengthening of the light.
sequence.voice: The book has an aside about marks. Water, wind and fire pass over grass and trees and leave them split and cut and weathered, and what you can see afterwards is the track those things took, which is not itself water, or wind, or fire. Everything in this shelter is a track of that kind. Nothing here is the process. Everything here is what the process left lying.

sequence.on_screen: Extreme macro, static, filled frame: one flake of quartz on a neutral surface, lit flat, the conchoidal ripple and the working edge legible. Held. Then a second flake, same framing, no camera move between them.
sequence.voice: Somebody struck this. You can see where. The word the book uses for the smallest real things is element, and its gloss is the flattest sentence in the whole compendium: element means own-nature, own-nature means empty, and empty means nissatta, nijjiva, not a being, not a living soul. The schoolbook puts it in four words: a thing that is not a being and not a person. That is not a verdict on anybody. It is a definition of what the pieces are.

sequence.on_screen: Back to wide. Static, from one side of the shelter, the whole empty floor across the frame and the darkness at the back where daylight stops. The slab of morning light is halfway out of the picture. No person in this one.
sequence.voice: The sources say the senses do not come from anywhere and do not go anywhere, and that they neither plan nor intend. And they give the inner senses a picture, which is this one: a village empty of anyone living in it, empty of permanence, of beauty, of pleasure and of self. It is a strange thing to be standing inside the simile.

sequence.on_screen: Macro again, static, shallow: a tooth from a sea fish, and beside it a marine shell bead, each held long in the frame, lit plainly, no turntable and no dramatic key. If these cannot be filmed, the same slot takes a grinding stone with ochre still in the dish, framed the same way.
sequence.voice: A shark's tooth, and a bead cut from a sea shell, in a shelter that stands today some thirty kilometres of forest from the nearest salt water. Somebody carried this. The sources say the concept of a being — a god, a man, a woman — is formed with the five aggregates as its basis: body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. None of that is on this tray, and four of the five could never be. What is on the tray is what those people handled. And a name is what conveys the concept: the sound of the word is ultimately real, and the name the sound carries is not. The names were said here. The sound went where sounds go. Nobody wrote one down, because writing had not been invented.

sequence.on_screen: Wide, static, from the same floor: the far end of the shelter where the modern shrine stands, the reclining figure and the whitewashed platform under the raw unworked rock of the ceiling. Filmed empty, or with people distant and unidentifiable. No observance is filmed, framed, waited for or lit.
sequence.voice: One name does reach this place. It arrived late, from outside, and the people who use it are not making a mistake. The sources sort concepts into kinds, and among them are the collective, the shape, the being, the direction, the time, and the one named by emptiness, a well, a cave. A name attaches to those, or to the ultimate things themselves. Every one of those names is doing real work. None of them is doing it for anyone who slept on this floor.

sequence.on_screen: The last frame is the first frame, held even longer. Inside looking out, late in the day, the light off the rock, the opening gone cool and the interior evenly grey. Nobody in it. The film ends on the shot it began on, unchanged.
sequence.voice: The book says it in one line, in the part about what is actually the case. There is a suffering that is felt, and no person who is the feeler of it; there is an action, and no doer standing behind it. Everywhere else you would have to take a name off something to see that. Here the names were said, and not one was kept.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests hand this location opposite halves of one sentence. C084 is the machinery of the name. Pannatti is convention other than mind and matter, and it is defined in the same breath as both the thing made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25]; the Margaya adds that most of what appears to people as the furniture of the world is pannatti, and that recognising it is what lets the ultimate be seen separately [C084-M:L5]. The name-concept is what is assigned either to an ultimate reality or to one of the meaning-concepts [C084-P:L47], and the concept of a being in particular is formed with the five aggregates as its basis [C084-M:L17]. The spoken sound is ultimately real; the name it carries is not [C084-M:L21]. C077 is the analysis of the basis on its own. It sorts everything there is four ways, into aggregates, bases, elements and truths [C077-P:L16-L24], insists that heap means collection and portion rather than label [C077-P:L36-L42], and glosses element down to nissatta, nijjiva, not a being and not a living soul [C077-P:L1447; C077-M:L56]. Put the two together and you get a pair: a basis, and a designation resting on it. Every other location in this group supplies a thing with its name on it and invites the film to separate them. This one supplies what thousands of lives handled with every designation absent, and not absent because anything was destroyed or because no name was ever used: the names were certainly spoken, and none survived, because nobody here could write and no institution lasted to remember. The basis the being-concept rests on, the five aggregates, four of them mental, is not on the table either and never could be; what is on the table is the evidence that people lived here, and the absence of their names in it. The compendium's answer to what a person is, performed at a site with no name available to remove.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That anonymity and loss are not the same thing, and that the difference is the whole film. C077 on its own would make a classification lecture. C084 on its own would make a film about words. Together, on a floor of ash and quartz, they produce the only claim worth making here: what the compendium says is underneath a name is exactly what is lying under this rock, and the reason it is legible is that no name placed on it was kept. The pairing also blocks the three cheap endings this site begs for. It is not a film about the dead, because the sources' interest is in the arrangement of items and not in anyone's passing. It is not a film about what people leave behind, because that framing is ruled out for this series and the compendium's own move is the opposite one. And it is not a film about how we are all the same underneath, because the same element list that finds hardness in bone and teeth finds it in iron and in every kind of stone [C077-P:L1475; C077-P:L1479-L1483], and gathers the two into one element [C077-P:L1485], for the stated reason that neither side holds a self, not that the two are one thing.

concept_links.why: The compendium is the subject and carries five of the eight beats. The objection that 'nobody here can be named' is true of any prehistoric site is fair, and it is why the film does not rest on anonymity: it rests on C077's own images, and this site is where they can be stood inside. The site is the compendium with its designations missing. Its four arrangements are set out at the head of the chapter [C077-P:L16-L24], and each is aimed at a different place a person puts the word I. The film uses four passages as images rather than as quotations. First, the definition of heap: a collection and a portion, expressly not a label, so that the wall of stacked sediment in the excavation is a heap in the technical sense and not a metaphor [C077-P:L36-L42], and the Margaya's flat statement that all the materiality there has ever been, divided as past and the rest, is taken by the mind as one collection and called by one word [C077-M:L10-L18]. Second, the gloss of element: own-nature, emptiness, nissatta and nijjiva, not a being and not a living soul [C077-P:L1447], put in four words by the schoolbook as a thing that is not a being and not a person [C077-M:L56]; this is the line the site has been carrying in sediment for forty thousand years. Third, the simile that hands the film its excavated section: water, wind and fire pass over grass and trees and what remains visible is the track they took, which is not water, wind or fire [C077-P:L2547-L2551]. That passage's own subject is ageing, which this film does not touch and does not narrate; only the first half of the simile, about marks and what made them, is used. Fourth, the picture given to the internal sense bases, a village empty of anyone living in it and empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure and self [C077-P:L1347], immediately after the statements that the bases neither come from anywhere nor go anywhere [C077-P:L1333–L1335] and neither plan nor intend [C077-P:L1337–L1345]. The film is shot standing inside that simile. The digest's limits are written into the beats and not parked in a caution. It is not you do not exist: what is dismantled is the view that takes form as mine, as me, as my self [C077-P:L1006-L1008], and the Margaya's stated use of the five is that it loosens the everyday I sentences [C077-M:L24]. It is not we are all one with nature, which this location invites hardest of all, because the element lists put hardness in bone and teeth and also in iron and in every kind of stone [C077-P:L1475; C077-P:L1479-L1483] and then gather both into one element [C077-P:L1485] precisely to show that neither side holds a self. It leaves no observer standing, since the eighteen elements are taught to remove the notion of a living soul sitting in the consciousness that knows an object [C077-P:L1853]. It is not a technique: the element contemplation is given to a monk of purified virtue who has learned it from a teacher [C077-P:L1493-L1497]. And it does not let the film say nobody really suffered here, because the compendium's position is that there is a suffering that is felt and no feeler standing behind it [C077-P:L2292-L2298]. One further line governs the style: the not-self mark stays hidden while things are not attended to as separated into their various elements, and while continuity covers them over [C077-P:L1389-L1393]. That is the argument for the macro register and for the refusal to move the camera. The digest flags an uncertainty in that same line about which factor does the concealing, so the film takes only the part about separating into elements.

Every piece of this concept the film uses is either physically present or conspicuously absent, which is the same evidence. Pannatti is convention other than mind and matter, and is both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25]; the Margaya adds that most of what appears to people as the world is pannatti, and that seeing it as such is what lets the ultimate be recognised separately [C084-M:L5]. The meaning-concepts are listed as the collective, the shape, the being, the direction, the time, the one named by emptiness such as a well or a cave, and the meditation sign [C084-P:L27-L41], and a name is what is assigned either to the ultimate realities or to those [C084-P:L47]. The hinge to C077 is the Margaya's definition of the being-concept as the one formed with the five aggregates as its basis [C084-M:L17]. That basis is not what is on the plinths here: four of the five aggregates are mental, and a shark's tooth or a bead is nobody's aggregates. What is on the plinths is what the people this concept was formed over handled, and none of their designations is on any of it; the film says so in beat six rather than letting the tray stand for the basis. The other load-bearing line is the separation of sound from name: the sound is a paramattha dhamma and the name it conveys is not [C084-M:L21]. Names were certainly spoken under this rock, thousands of them; sound is real and momentary and none of it was written, so nothing carried them. That is the film's cleanest fact and it comes straight out of the source. The six ways a name stands to its basis [C084-P:L49-L71; C084-M:L23-L35] are read but deliberately not built on, because the third of them, a really existent quality used to designate something that is not, is the ground of another film in this group; here the point is prior to the sixfold scheme, that no name-concept of any of the six kinds is available at all. The digest's guards travel with the link. The existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not a scheme of true and false; conventional wholes stay valid in their own domain, since the division test shows only that what dissolves under analysis is a concept, not that it is fake [C084-M:L7]; and no monk, pilgrim or official at this site is told that the name they use for it is wrong.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a name is not a small copy of a person stored somewhere. The demonstration is on screen and needs no belief: a wall of layers, a chipped stone, a tooth from a sea fish carried in from a coast that today lies some thirty kilometres away. Thousands of people handled these things and said each other's names over them, and not one name is in them. What the sources say a person-name rests on, body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, is not on the table either, and most of it could never be. The absence is not a gap in the record but a fact about what names are made of: they were said, and nothing here could keep them.
what_must_be_real: No human remains are filmed. Not bone, not a skull, not a tooth from a person, not a cast, not a museum display of any of them, and not a photograph of one on a wall panel; if a display case at the site or at the Department of Archaeology contains human material, the camera does not go there and the shot list does not route past it. The subject is the shelter, the excavated section, the sediment, the stone tools and the food debris. The film is not a memorial and contains no burial, no grief, no ancestry and no what-they-left-behind; nobody is mourned, because nobody is named and the film's entire claim is that this is a fact about naming and not a loss. The excavated section is filmed exactly as the archaeologists left it, including the shoring, the string lines, the backfill and the litter; no layer is brushed, wetted, raked or cut back to make it read, and if it is backfilled it is filmed backfilled or not at all. Artefacts are filmed where they are, in whatever light the shelter gives, with the permission of whoever holds them, and are never rearranged into a composition or lit theatrically. The shrine is a working shrine: no act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repeated or lit, nobody at the site is framed as an exhibit of anything, and nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera appears in the film. The person who gives the wide frame its scale does so knowingly and by agreement and is not identifiable as anyone in particular. The dating, the measurements and the primacy claim are stated at the level of confidence the literature actually supports, on screen as well as in the voice.
position_hint: Late-middle of the group, and the group's one film with no monument, no carving, no inscription and no tradition in it. It should follow at least one film in which a name is taken off a thing, so that the viewer already has the move before being shown a place where there is nothing to take off. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Elegy. This is the largest risk by a long way. A dark cave, deep time and vanished people will pull every instinct toward mourning, and the film fails the moment it reads as elegiac. The word for the subject is anonymity, not loss. The series has already ruled that legacy and remembrance are not the teaching, and that bar is fully live here.

Death, burial, mortality and human remains. The excavations produced skeletal material and secondary burials, and the film uses none of it, films none of it and narrates none of it. Anything that turns the shelter into a place where people died rather than a place where people lived is out.

The 2017 landslides. On 26 May 2017 landslides in the surrounding division killed about twenty-two villagers, with the village where the approach begins at the base of one slide, and monks were evacuated from the temple on landslide-risk advice. The landslide is never a subject, never mentioned in the voice, and no one affected is filmed; no frame of the hillside, the forest, the steps or the rain is composed, paced or graded in a bereavement register, and the rain-curtain shot must not read as the weather that killed people. The crew's own safety comes first: no climb or work in the shelter under an active landslide warning.
Deep-time awe that lands as a lesson about human smallness or humility. The sources are not making that argument and the voice must not smuggle it in at the end of a wide shot.

We are all one with nature, and we are all the same underneath. The element lists match bone to iron and to every kind of stone [C077-P:L1475; C077-P:L1479-L1483] and gather both into one element [C077-P:L1485], and the digest is explicit that the point of the match is that neither side contains a self, not that the two merge. On a film whose subject is a rock this is a standing danger in every frame.

Sliding from the analysis into you do not exist or nobody was really there. What is dismantled is the view that takes form as mine and as me [C077-P:L1006-L1008; C077-M:L24]; the people who lived here were people in ordinary speech and the film says so plainly.
No self, therefore nobody really suffered. The compendium says the opposite: the suffering is real and only its owner is missing [C077-P:L2292-L2298].
Removing the self and quietly leaving an observer in its place; the eighteen elements are taught against exactly that [C077-P:L1853].

Wellness drift, which arrives here as a cave-and-silence meditation piece. The element contemplation is placed inside monastic discipline with a teacher and preconditions [C077-P:L1493-L1497], and the shelter is not offered as a place to feel anything.

Nothing is real. The sources keep sound, colour, feeling and mind fully real and keep conventional wholes valid in their own domain; the division test shows what dissolves under analysis, not what is fake [C084-M:L7; C084-M:L5]. The existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not true and false.

Telling anyone at the site that the name they use for it is only a sound, or implying that the shrine is a later intrusion on the real subject. The digest forbids correcting a participant's usage, and the community using the shelter now is not part of the argument.

Presenting the dating or the oldest-in-South-Asia claim as settled. The published figures differ by thousands of years depending on which layer, which sample and which paper, and the cave's own measurements differ by a factor of two between the field literature and the popular accounts.

Becoming an archaeology documentary: a history of the excavations, a cast of archaeologists, a reconstruction, a chart of phases. The film is a rock shelter, its scale, its dark and its light, with a voice explaining that everything in it is a basis with no name on it.

Taking another film's ground in this group. Three other ideas share this concept pair: one walks between a colonnade whose building is gone and a stupa of millions of bricks that lost half its height, under names that did not change; one keeps an exact count of seven carved figures whose names are all proposals; one follows a single name taken from the colour of the ground at a cape. This one must not count anything, must not build on a mass of identical units, must not derive a name from a quality, and must not frame the absence as a name that used to be here and was lost.
Style collision. If the camera moves, or a drone flies the cliff, or the film acquires a mid-shot grammar, the one thing that distinguishes it from the rest of the group is gone.

Access and the dark. The interior is genuinely dark at the back, the excavation is a hole with railings around it in a space shared with worshippers and visitors, and no lighting rig, cable run or tripod position is worth obstructing either.
drop_if: The film cannot be made without filming human remains, or the only way to show the stratigraphy runs through a display containing them.
The temple does not want the shelter filmed, or will permit it only on terms that make the resident community or worshippers into an exhibit.
The excavated sections are backfilled, fenced or hoarded over, and no legible cut face, section drawing or in-place artefact can be filmed, leaving the film with a wide shot and no macro register.
The site turns out to be so crowded during all available hours that the long static frames cannot be held and the consent floor cannot be met.
The whole treatment can only be delivered with camera movement or an aerial, which would collapse it into the other films in the group.
The shelter or its approach is closed or restricted on landslide-safety grounds, or the film can only be made in a way that brings the 2017 landslide into it.

connections.note: Same concept pair, opposite condition. That film walks between two monuments whose names outlived what they named — a colonnade whose building is gone and a stupa that lost half its height — and it has also absorbed the group's counted-heap film. This one has a place where names were used every day and none was kept. The pairing only works if this film never says a name here was lost.

Same concept pair, deliberately different subject. That film has an enumeration of carved figures whose identifications are disputed; this one has no carving and no dispute about identity, because there is no identification to argue over.

Same concept pair, deliberately different ground. That film is one name, taken from the colour of the ground at a cape and laid over a whole country, resting on a really existent quality; this one is ground that carried thousands of names and kept none. No name-from-a-quality here, and no absence of names there.

The opening film has one thing carrying four names at once. This one has forty thousand years of people carrying none, and it should sit far enough away from the opening that the viewer has already watched a name come off something.

selection.reason: The group's deep-prehistory film and its only location with no monument, no carving, no inscription and no tradition in it: rock, sediment and time, carrying the compendium's own answer to what a person is with no name available to take off.

review.note: Revised on 2026-09-26 after a GRP-01 audit; the location and concepts are unchanged and the film is now the recommended eighth film for the group, so this is the version Chathura is being asked to judge. The audit found an internal contradiction and it has been resolved: some lines said names were spoken here continuously while the logline, the last beat and the concept merge said no name was ever applied. Only the keeping of names is missing, and the logline, beat eight ('Here the names were said, and not one was kept') and the concept merge now say so. Beat six no longer says 'the basis is on this tray': the sources' basis for the concept of a being is the five aggregates, four of them mental, and a shark's tooth is nobody's aggregates, so the tray is now what those people handled and the voice says the basis could never be on it. Beat six also now says the coast is some thirty kilometres away 'today', since the Pleistocene coast lay further off. Beat seven no longer calls the attribution of the site's name to a traveller a story the record does not support, because that verges on telling the people who use the name that it is wrong; the neutral clause that they are not making a mistake stays. The bracketed citations have been taken out of every spoken line, as in the opening film, and remain in the concept links, the merge and the historical thread; one citation range for 'neither plan nor intend' was corrected to the lines that carry it. In the research, the 'five skulls' could not be confirmed and was withdrawn, the shark teeth are no longer credited to the 2020 bow-and-arrow paper, whose coverage reports three shell and three ochre beads, and the 2017 landslides that killed about twenty-two villagers around the approach are now in the risks, the access note and drop_if, as a safety hazard and a register the film must never enter, never as a subject. What Chathura is being asked to judge is chiefly the audit's strongest objection, which the research note states in full: that 'nobody here can be named' is true of any prehistoric site. The film's answer is that it rests on the primary concept's own images — the empty village of the sense bases, the heap as collection, the element as not a being — and that this is a single roofed dwelling one can stand inside and hold in one frame, with the excavated section in the same room. Whether that answer is strong enough, and whether the site is still open and safe after 2017, are the open questions. Everything in the location block remains desk research, unchecked on the ground.

suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place in the pool that delivers the concept and the picture in the same frame while sharing no archetype with anything else in the group. The picture is a single natural overhang large enough that the only honest way to shoot it is one enormous held frame from inside looking out, with a human figure small enough inside it to give the rock its real size; there is no monument in it, nothing carved, and no aerial reveal to reach for. The concept is the site's actual condition. Excavation has produced a long Late Pleistocene and Holocene occupation, the earliest fossil appearance of Homo sapiens reported anywhere in South Asia, quartz microliths, bone points, ochre, grinding stones, freshwater and forest food debris, and marine shell beads and shark teeth carried in from a coast tens of kilometres away. What it has not produced, and structurally cannot, is a single name. No inscription, no chronicle, no lineage, no tradition: writing arrived tens of thousands of years too late. The compendium's whole method is to take the name off a person and describe what is left as an arrangement of momentary items, and its textbooks gloss element as not a being, not a person, not a living soul. This is that description at a place where every name that was used has gone, and what those people handled is excavated, catalogued and standing on a plinth in the same shelter.

historical_thread.story:
The shelter is a single enormous overhang in a gneiss cliff in the lowland wet zone of southwestern Sri Lanka, in evergreen and semi-evergreen rainforest, and it is not a cave in the speleological sense: it is an abri, a roofed recess with a mouth open to the weather, and the published archaeological description gives the mouth as about thirty metres across with an average of about twenty metres of clear height above the present floor, the shelter running back roughly ten metres into the cliff, and two main chambers designated Shelter A and Shelter B. Popular and tourist accounts give quite different figures, commonly around 175 feet high, 160 to 175 feet wide and 200 to 282 feet long, and one caving reference gives a 53-metre portal and a 60-metre length. Alongside those runs the claim that it is the largest natural rock cave in South Asia and that three thousand, or three thousand five hundred, people could shelter under it at once. That figure is repeated everywhere and no source found in this research attributes it to a measurement or a survey.

The name is an attribution rather than a record. It is given to the Chinese Buddhist monk known as Fa-Hien or Faxian, who was in the island in the early fifth century CE; the standard reference position is that there is no archaeological or historical evidence that he was ever at this shelter. A separate local tradition credits a monk called Porogama Thera with clearing the shelter and founding the temple in it, and points to a large iron implement called the yakula, kept at the foot of the reclining figure, as his tool. That tradition is oral and unverified. A Buddhist shrine has occupied part of the shelter for a long time, and the place was in active use as a cave temple when archaeologists first recorded it; the shrine today has a reclining Buddha reported at between about thirteen and twelve metres long, a whitewashed platform, and a monk's dwelling built against the rock. The two histories run side by side on the same floor, and the older one is the one with no names in it.

The archaeological record is recent, well published and still moving. S. U. Deraniyagala of the Sri Lanka Department of Archaeology recorded the site in 1968, while it was in use as a temple. W. H. Wijeyapala excavated in two places, Shelter A and Shelter B, from 1986, and Nimal Perera, Oshan Wedage and Deraniyagala worked there between about 2009 and 2012, with further campaigns reported in 2013 and a collaboration from around 2019 involving the Department of Archaeology, the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History and Griffith University. Human skeletal material recovered from the earlier campaigns was studied at Cornell University by Kenneth A. R. Kennedy and Joanne L. Zahorsky, assigned to anatomically modern Homo sapiens, and carbon-dated in the United States, and the figures quoted for it vary. Different publications give the earliest human fossils from the site as approximately 30,600, 37,000 or 38,000 years old, and the site is described in the literature as the earliest fossil appearance of Homo sapiens in South Asia. The reassessed sequence divides the deposits into five stratigraphic layers and four occupation phases: Phase D in the Late Pleistocene at roughly 48,000 to 34,000 calibrated years before present, Phase C in the terminal Pleistocene at about 13,000 to 12,000, Phase B in the early Holocene at about 8,700 to 8,000, and Phase A in the middle Holocene at about 6,000 to 4,000, with a gap across the Last Glacial Maximum roughly between 28,000 and 13,000. The deposits themselves are described as pebbly loams and clayey and sandy silts with laminated ash, read as intermittent rather than continuous occupation.

What came out of the ground is a rainforest life, and a very specific one. Analysis of 14,485 bone fragments found that small mammals make up over ninety per cent of the identified animal remains, with monkeys and tree squirrels alone over seventy per cent, hunted selectively and at prime age. There are microliths overwhelmingly of quartz, bone and antler tools, and in 2020 Michelle Langley and colleagues published a microscopic study of 130 bone points from levels dated between about 48,000 and 34,000 years ago, arguing from impact fractures that they were arrow tips, which would make them the earliest evidence for bow-and-arrow hunting outside Africa. Press coverage of that paper reports three beads made from sea shell and three made from ochre, and the institutions' own release describes coloured beads from red, yellow and metallic ochre and shell beads traded from the coast. Shark teeth are not attributed to that paper in any source reached here; they are reported, with beads of marine shell, shark vertebrae and a shell pendant, 'from the earliest cultural layers' in the summary of the excavations published on archaeology.lk. Red ochre was found ground into stone querns. Lagoon molluscs of the species Potamides cingulatus in deposits around 20,000 years old have been read as evidence for rock salt brought from lagoons in the southeast of the island, over a hundred kilometres away. The nearest sea coast today is roughly thirty kilometres west of the shelter; at the lower sea levels of the Pleistocene it lay further off.

So the site holds, in one deposit, a technology, a diet, an ornament industry, a pigment, a long-distance supply line and a record of who was hunted and how. It holds no names, though names were certainly used in it. There is no script anywhere in the sequence, because there was none to have; there is no chronicle, because the island's chronicles begin tens of thousands of years later and say nothing about this place; there is no lineage and no tradition that reaches back into the occupation. The one name the place carries now belongs to a fifth-century traveller whose connection to it the record does not support. Everything in the shelter is something a person handled. Nothing in it is a designation.

The hillside is also a place of recent loss, and the record notes it so that the film can keep clear of it. In the early hours of 26 May 2017 landslides in the Bulathsinhala division killed about twenty-two villagers — the Sunday Times gives 22 and the Daily FT 21 — with Yatagampitiya, where the approach to the shelter begins, at the base of one of the slides. The National Building Research Organisation declared the area landslide-prone, the monks were evacuated from the temple, cracks were reported near the entrance to the cave, and the minister responsible for the Department of Archaeology asked for a report. The landslide is not part of this film.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C084 defines a name as half of a pair. Pannatti is convention other than mind and matter, and it is called pannatti both because it is made known and because it makes known [C084-P:L25]: a thing designated, and a designation. The Margaya adds the part that matters for a site with no writing in it, that the spoken sound is a paramattha dhamma while the name the sound conveys is not [C084-M:L21]. Sound is real and it is momentary. Under this rock, for something like forty thousand years, names were spoken continuously; every one of them was real when it was said and none of them was recorded, because writing did not exist, and so nothing carried a single one of them out of the air. That is not a gap in the archaeological record. It is the source's own account of what a spoken name is, running at the scale of the Late Pleistocene, and it is the reason this site can demonstrate something no monument can.

Second, the sources say exactly what the concept of a being is built on: it is the pannatti formed with the five aggregates as its basis [C084-M:L17], and the name-concept is what is assigned to an ultimate reality or to one of the meaning-concepts [C084-P:L47]. That is a two-part structure. This site does not supply the first part — four of the five aggregates are mental and none of them lies in a trench — but it supplies what the people it was formed over handled, excavated, dated and catalogued, and nothing whatever of the second. The compendium then describes the first part on its own terms: everything that exists sorted into aggregates, bases, elements and truths [C077-P:L16-L24], with heap meaning a collection and a portion rather than a label [C077-P:L36-L42], and all the materiality there has ever been, divided as past and future and present, taken by the mind as one collection and called by one word [C077-M:L10-L18]. An excavated section is that sentence made visible: a stack of collections, one above the other, with nothing in it that is anybody. And the definition the whole film rests on is flat and unsentimental: element means own-nature, own-nature means empty, and empty means nissatta, nijjiva, not a being, not a living soul [C077-P:L1447], which the schoolbook compresses to a thing that is not a being and not a person [C077-M:L56]. At any other site that line is something the voice asserts over footage. Here it is the condition of the evidence.

Third, the site is the sources' own simile, twice over, and this is what makes the binding specific rather than atmospheric. The internal sense bases are to be known as a village empty of anyone living in it, empty of permanence, of beauty, of pleasure and of self [C077-P:L1347], stated immediately after the points that the bases come from nowhere and go nowhere [C077-P:L1333–L1335] and neither plan nor intend [C077-P:L1337–L1345]. This film is shot standing inside an empty human habitation, which is the image the text reaches for, and the camera does not move because the simile is not about coming or going. And the stratigraphy is the other simile: water, wind and fire pass over grass and trees, and what remains visible afterwards is the track those things took, which is not itself water, wind or fire [C077-P:L2547-L2551]. Every layer in the cut face is a track of that kind. The passage's own subject in the book is ageing, which this film does not use and does not narrate; only the half about marks and what made them is taken, and taken because the location performs it literally.

What binds hardest is the negative case. The grasping the analysis dismantles is stated in the first person: this form is mine, this is me, this is my self [C077-P:L1006-L1008], and the Margaya's version is the everyday sentences, I am beautiful, I am tall [C077-M:L24]. Every one of those sentences was said under this rock, thousands of times a day, for forty thousand years, and not one of them survives. So the film is not able to take a name off anybody even if it wanted to, and that inability is the argument. It also fixes the film's discipline: the not-self mark stays hidden while things are not attended to as separated into their various elements [C077-P:L1389-L1393], which is precisely what the macro register does and what a moving camera would undo. And the guard the site most needs comes from the same chapter. The element lists put hardness in bone and teeth and also in iron and in every kind of stone [C077-P:L1475; C077-P:L1479-L1483], and gather the internal and the external into one element [C077-P:L1485] for the stated reason that neither side holds a self, not because the two are one thing. On a film about a rock and the people who slept on it, that distinction is the difference between the concept and a cosmic platitude. The last thing the sources refuse is the film's most tempting ending: there is a suffering that is felt and no person who is the feeler, an action and no doer [C077-P:L2292-L2298]. Nobody here is being told they did not exist. What is missing is the owner, and at this one site the owner's name is missing too, which is as close as a location will ever come to the argument itself.
what_is_certain: The site is a rock shelter in a gneiss cliff at Yatagampitiya, near Bulathsinhala, Kalutara District, Western Province, in lowland evergreen and semi-evergreen rainforest, described in the archaeological literature as approximately 75 km southeast of Colombo.

The peer-reviewed description of the shelter gives an east-facing entrance of about 30 m by 20 m, an interior extending roughly 10 m into the cliff, and two main chambers designated Shelter A and Shelter B.
The site was recorded in 1968 by S. U. Deraniyagala of the Sri Lanka Department of Archaeology, at a time when the shelter was in use as a Buddhist cave temple.

W. H. Wijeyapala excavated at two locations in the shelter from 1986, and further excavation was carried out by Nimal Perera, Oshan Wedage and S. U. Deraniyagala between about 2009 and 2012, with later work reported in 2013 and a collaboration from around 2019 between the Department of Archaeology, the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History and Griffith University.

Human skeletal material from the site was studied at Cornell University by Kenneth A. R. Kennedy and Joanne L. Zahorsky and assigned to anatomically modern Homo sapiens. The dates quoted for it differ: see what_is_disputed.
The site is described in the published literature as the earliest fossil appearance of anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, in South Asia.

The reassessed sequence gives five stratigraphic layers and four occupation phases: Phase D, Late Pleistocene, about 48,000 to 34,000 cal BP; Phase C, terminal Pleistocene, about 13,000 to 12,000 cal BP; Phase B, early Holocene, about 8,700 to 8,000 cal BP; Phase A, middle Holocene, about 6,000 to 4,000 cal BP, with a hiatus across the Last Glacial Maximum, roughly 28,000 to 13,000 cal BP.
The deposits are described as pebbly loams and clayey and sandy silts with laminated ash, interpreted as intermittent or episodic occupation.

Analysis of 14,485 animal bone fragments found that small mammals make up over ninety per cent of the identified remains, with monkeys and tree squirrels over seventy per cent, and that prime-aged adults were targeted.
The stone tool assemblage is dominated by quartz microliths, and the site also produced bone and antler tools, ochre, and grinding stones with red ochre in them.

Michelle Langley and colleagues published a microscopic study of 130 bone points from levels dated between about 48,000 and 34,000 years ago in Science Advances in 2020 (6(24):eaba3831), arguing from impact damage that they were arrow tips and describing them as the earliest evidence for bow-and-arrow technology outside Africa. Press coverage of the paper reports three beads made from sea shell and three made from ochre, and the release by the authors' institutions describes coloured beads from red, yellow and metallic ochre and shell beads traded from the coast.

Marine material is present in the deposits: the summary of the excavations on archaeology.lk reports beads of marine shell and shark vertebrae, shark teeth and a shell pendant 'from the earliest cultural layers', and Langley and colleagues report shell beads traded from the coast.

Lagoon molluscs of the species Potamides cingulatus occur in deposits dated to around 20,000 years ago and have been interpreted as evidence for rock salt brought from lagoons in the southeast of the island, over 100 km away.

A Buddhist shrine occupies part of the shelter today, with a large reclining Buddha figure, a whitewashed platform, an iron implement known as the yakula kept at its foot, and a monk's dwelling built against the rock. The shelter was already in use as a cave temple at the time of the 1968 recording.
There is no inscription, no carving, no chronicle entry and no documented lineage or tradition connecting any named person to the prehistoric occupation of the shelter.

Photographs on Wikimedia Commons dated 2010 show an open excavation pit with timber shoring and railings inside the shelter, and grinding stones set out on low plinths, which indicates that at that date the excavated area was not backfilled.

On 26 May 2017 landslides in the Bulathsinhala division of Kalutara District killed about twenty-two villagers, with Yatagampitiya at the base of one slide; the National Building Research Organisation declared the area landslide-prone, monks were evacuated from the Pahiyangala temple, and cracks were reported near the cave entrance.
what_is_disputed: The dimensions. The peer-reviewed field description gives roughly 30 m wide by 20 m high with a 10 m interior; popular and tourist accounts give about 175 ft (53 m) high, 160 to 175 ft wide and 200 to 282 ft long; a caving reference gives a 53 m portal and a 60 m length. These are not reconcilable and the film uses the field figures and says the others are in circulation.

The claim that it is the largest natural rock cave, or the largest rock shelter, in South Asia. It is repeated in almost every account. No source found in this research attributes the claim to a survey or a comparative measurement, and the wording varies between largest cave in Sri Lanka, largest natural rock cave in South Asia and one of the largest natural rock formations in Asia.

The capacity figure. Three thousand is the usual number, three thousand five hundred also appears, and nothing found here indicates how either was arrived at. It is an estimate in local circulation, not a measurement.

The date of the earliest human remains. Published and quoted figures include approximately 30,600, about 37,000 and about 38,000 years before present, depending on the sample and the publication; occupation of the shelter is variously given as beginning about 48,000, 47,000 or 45,000 years ago, and popular accounts give a habitation range of 35,000 to 60,000 years. The film does not settle this and does not state a single figure as the date.

The geology. The peer-reviewed description says gneiss; one travel source says granite; the English Wikipedia article describes a limestone formation produced by corrosion. Gneiss is the figure from the field literature and is what this block uses.
The elevation. Figures found include about 122 m, about 130 m, 400 ft and 45 m above sea level. Not resolved.

Which layers the marine ornaments come from, and who reported them. An earlier version of this record attributed shark teeth and marine shell beads from terminal Pleistocene levels to Langley and colleagues (2020); no source reached confirms that attribution and it is withdrawn. Coverage of that paper mentions shell beads, not shark teeth. archaeology.lk places shark teeth, shark vertebrae, marine shell beads and a shell pendant in the earliest cultural layers. The exact layer and date of the shark teeth were not confirmed.

The number of skulls. An earlier version of this record said five human skulls were studied at Cornell; neither the Wikipedia article nor the archaeology.lk summary gives a count, and no source reached here confirms five. The count is withdrawn and could not be confirmed.

The distance to the sea. The 100 km figure that appears in several accounts refers specifically to the inferred source of lagoon molluscs and rock salt in the southeast of the island, not to the nearest coast. The nearest sea coast is roughly 30 km west, a distance measured off the map from the published coordinates rather than taken from any source, and a present-day distance: at the lower sea levels of the Late Pleistocene the coast lay further west, so the distance when the marine objects were carried in was greater, by an amount not established here. The voice says 'today'. A separate and often-confused figure of about 40 km from the coast belongs in the literature to a different inland cave site and is not used here.

The name. The attribution to the Chinese monk Fa-Hien or Faxian, who was in the island in the early fifth century CE, is described in the standard reference literature as a legend with no archaeological or historical evidence behind it. The tradition crediting the monk Porogama Thera with clearing the shelter and founding the temple, and the story attached to the yakula, are oral and unverified.

The current state of the excavated areas. Commons photographs from 2010 show an open, shored pit, and one account refers to a deep shaft still visible; whether those sections are open, fenced, covered or backfilled in 2026 is unknown and is listed as an unknown rather than a finding.

Nothing in this record adjudicates anything about the people who lived here. The dating establishes when deposits formed and when samples died, not who anyone was, and the absence of names is a fact about writing and about survival of evidence, not a finding about the occupants.

The 2017 death toll. The Sunday Times (18 June 2017) gives 22 villagers dead in the Bulathsinhala landslides of 26 May; the Daily FT (8 June 2017) says the landslide 'buried 21 persons alive'. Both figures are recorded; neither enters the film.

what_to_film: The one wide frame, from inside the shelter looking out, with the arch of the overhang across the top of the picture and a single person standing near the drip line for scale. This is the film and everything else is built around getting it. Shot on a long lens and a short lens, from two or three fixed positions, held for minutes at a time, and never moved within a take.

The same frame at four times of day, so the light can be cut as a single slow change with no camera move: the slab of morning sun on the floor, its withdrawal, the flat even shade of the middle of the day, and the cool of late afternoon.

The cut face of the excavation, filmed at macro, static, in available light: the bands of ash, loam and pebbly silt, the timber shoring, the string lines, the backfill and the dust, exactly as they are.
Quartz flakes and microliths at the highest magnification the lens will give, filled frame, lit flat, one at a time, each held; and the working edge, where the conchoidal ripple is legible.
A grinding stone with red ochre still in the dish, on its plinth, in the shelter's own light.

A shark's tooth and a marine shell bead, where they are held and with permission, framed as plainly as the quartz. If they cannot be filmed, the slot goes to the grinding stones and the film says nothing about the sea it cannot show.
The dark at the back of the shelter where daylight stops, filmed as darkness rather than lifted in the grade.
The rock overhead: water-worn flutings, staining, the raw curve of the roof, close and static.
The shrine end of the shelter, filmed as architecture, empty or with people distant and unidentifiable, and without waiting for or framing any act of worship.
The approach, for the first two minutes of the film: the steps, the rubber and secondary forest, the cliff appearing through the canopy, all from fixed positions.

Rain past the mouth in the wet season, from inside, one locked frame: lit rain in the opening, dry grey floor in the foreground. Only on a day with no landslide warning in force for the district, and never framed or graded as foreboding.
Nothing aerial. No drone material is shot for this film, and if aerial coverage exists it is not used.
suggested_location.access: On foot. A road reaches Yatagampitiya, about 5 km from Bulathsinhala town and roughly 75 km southeast of Colombo, and the shelter is reached from there by a long flight of stone steps reported as a climb of about twenty minutes. Reports say entry is free and the site is open in daylight hours, with modest dress requested in the shrine area and a torch useful for the back of the shelter. It is a working temple as well as an archaeological site, and access for a crew, for tripods and for lighting is a matter for the temple and for the Department of Archaeology and has not been sought. The hillside is landslide-prone. On 26 May 2017 landslides in the surrounding division killed about twenty-two villagers, the National Building Research Organisation declared the area at risk, monks were evacuated from the temple and cracks were reported near the entrance. Any wet-season work, and the rain-curtain shot in particular, depends on the Organisation's current warnings for Kalutara District and on the temple's advice: the crew does not climb to or work in the shelter while a landslide warning is in force, and if the shot can only be had under one, the shot is dropped. Whether any part of the shelter or the steps has been restricted since 2017 is unknown.
suggested_location.best_time: January to March is the drier window in this part of the wet zone and the easiest for the climb and for leeches; the southwest monsoon from May to September and the second wet spell around October bring the heaviest rain and the rain-curtain shot, and also the landslide risk: wet-season days are usable only when no landslide warning is in force. Within the day, the east-facing mouth means the raking light across the floor exists only in the first two hours or so after sunrise; from mid-morning the interior is in even, unchanging shade, which is what the long static frames and the macro work need.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search carried out on 25 September 2026 and none of it has been checked on the ground or against a printed edition. The site description, the phase and layer scheme, the dates, the faunal analysis and the excavation history are taken from the peer-reviewed literature as reproduced on PMC and archaeology.lk, chiefly Wedage and colleagues in Nature Communications (2019) and Langley and colleagues in Science Advances (2020, 6(24):eaba3831); the Science Advances page itself returned HTTP 403 and its contents are quoted here through secondary summaries and search indexing rather than from the article. Dimensions, elevation, capacity, the temple, the yakula and the access details come from Sri Lankan heritage and travel sites and from the English Wikipedia article, and where those conflict with the field literature the conflict is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than resolved; two of the travel sources (travelkalutara.com and atlasobscura.com) returned HTTP 403 and are cited only for material that reached this research through search summaries, which is why they are listed but not leaned on. The coordinates are the Wikipedia infobox values, 6 degrees 36 minutes 6 seconds north by 80 degrees 13 minutes 6 seconds east. The figure of roughly 30 km to the nearest sea coast is my own measurement off those coordinates and is not taken from any source; the 100 km figure in the literature refers to the inferred southeastern lagoon source of the salt and molluscs, and a 40 km coastal-contact figure that circulates in the same searches belongs to a different inland cave and is deliberately excluded. Every claim in the brief that started this rewrite was checked: the largest-in-South-Asia claim and the three thousand capacity are real and ubiquitous but unsourced, and are held in what_is_disputed; the earliest fossil appearance of Homo sapiens in South Asia is supported by the published literature; the sea fish, salt and shark teeth are supported by the summaries, with the qualification that the marine material is shark teeth and vertebrae, marine shell beads and a shell pendant rather than a marine bony-fish assemblage, and that the salt is an inference from lagoon molluscs rather than a direct find. The east-facing aspect of the mouth comes from the field literature and corrects the assumption in the brief that the overhang faces north or south; it changes the shooting plan, because it puts the raking light in the first hours after sunrise only. Seven images were found on Wikimedia Commons, confirmed through the API by title and imageinfo, and every one of them was downloaded and looked at before being listed here: none of them shows human remains, and none was selected from a description alone. The two images of grinding stones (Pahiyangala 04 and 05) also happen to be the best available evidence that an open, timber-shored excavation pit existed inside the shelter in 2010, which is recorded above as evidence for that date and not for the present. No permission, contact or access of any kind has been sought. Revision, 26 September 2026, after a GRP-01 audit. Three attributions were corrected: the 'five skulls' could not be confirmed in any source and was withdrawn; the shark teeth, previously credited to Langley and colleagues, are reported only by the archaeology.lk summary of the excavations ('from the earliest cultural layers'), while coverage of the Langley paper (Science News) reports three shell beads and three ochre beads; the thirty-kilometre distance is now said to be a present-day figure. The faunal counts, phases and dates from Wedage and colleagues (2019, PMC6381157) were not in question and stand. The 2017 landslides were confirmed from the Sunday Times (18 June 2017), Hiru News and the Daily FT (8 June 2017); the Roar article already cited is titled for this 'modern tragedy' and the earlier record never said what it was. They are now in the risks, the access note and drop_if, as a hazard and a register the film must keep out of, never as a subject. Two readings in the record were also wrong on the sources' own terms and have been changed. The film said in places that no name was ever applied here while also saying, correctly, that names were spoken continuously; only the keeping of names is missing, and the logline, beat eight and the concept merge now say so. And beat six said the being-concept's basis was on the tray: the C084 digest's basis for a being is the five aggregates [C084-M:L17], four of them mental, and no object is anyone's aggregates, so the tray is now what those people handled. The strongest objection to this film, stated plainly: 'nobody here can be named' is true of every prehistoric site on earth, so anonymity alone does not make this the place. The film's answer is that it does not rest on anonymity but on C077, the primary concept, whose own images this site lets the camera stand inside. The internal sense bases are 'a village empty of anyone living in it' [C077-P:L1347]: most prehistoric sites are open scatters or pits, and this one is a single roofed dwelling space one can stand in and hold in one frame. Heap as collection and not label [C077-P:L36–L42] is the exposed section in the same room. Element as 'not a being, not a living soul' [C077-P:L1447] is the flake. If the section has been backfilled, C077 is carried by the simile and the macro alone and the film is weaker; that is recorded in drop_if and the unknowns. The objection is not fully answered, and Chathura should weigh it.

unknowns: No permission, contact or access has been sought or confirmed, at the temple, at the Department of Archaeology, or with any of the excavation teams. Everything here is a research direction.

Whether the excavated sections are still open, shored and legible, or have been fenced, covered or backfilled since the 2010 photographs, is genuinely unknown, and the film's entire macro register depends on the answer.

Whether any excavated material can be filmed, where it is held, and on what conditions, is unknown. The human remains are curated by the Department of Archaeology and are not wanted; the quartz, the bone points, the ochre, the grinding stones and the marine ornaments are, and their availability has not been checked.
Whether a crew may bring tripods, a macro rig or any lighting into a working shrine, and during which hours, is unknown, as is whether filming requires a permit for a protected archaeological site.
Drone flight is not wanted for this film and is not planned; whether it would be permitted at all is unknown and irrelevant.

How dark the interior actually is at the back at each time of day, whether the morning light reaches the excavated section or only the outer floor, and whether the shelter is quiet enough at any hour for takes of several minutes, have not been checked on the ground.
How busy the site is, in which months and at which hours, and whether the consent floor can be met while filming a shared space, is unknown.

The published dimensions cannot be reconciled from a desk and would need measuring, or at least a single authoritative survey figure, before anything about the scale of the overhang is stated on screen.

Whether the shelter, the steps or the temple have been restricted since the 2017 landslide evacuation, whether the cracks reported near the entrance have been assessed or repaired, and what the landslide-warning regime means for a crew on a wet-season day, are unknown.

The location was proposed by Claude, for Chathura to confirm or reject, after the previous proposal was replaced to break the group's Buddhist-monument monoculture, and all of its supporting detail is desk research by web search and unverified. The concept reading is taken from the C077 and C084 digests and their cited source lines. No scene or shot is decided here.
